narrative: The model estimated a 47.0% chance that you will leave in the near term. In this promotion process, that was treated as enough leave risk to deny the promotion, even though it is close to a coin flip rather than a certainty. The most important signal was your overall years of experience: at 1–5 years, this was the strongest single influence and it worked in your favor, pushing the prediction toward staying; this is common among employees predicted to stay (50.4%). The next two signals worked against you. You reported having other job opportunities, which increased the leave risk; most comparable stayers did not report this (76.7%). You also described work-life balance as difficult, which further pushed toward leaving; most stayers reported medium balance (62.0%). So the denial reflects a close call: your experience was stabilizing, but external opportunities and difficult balance added leaving pressure that outweighed it alongside other profile factors. Next, the organization should discuss workload, flexibility, and career path with you, and check whether the promotion itself would improve retention. You should ask for clear promotion criteria and raise work-life balance concerns, because addressing them may reduce the risk the model is flagging.
